title: The Damascus road (Acts 9:1–19)
hookLine: Saul the persecutor is knocked down, blinded, and becomes Paul

lines: SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?
cards: Saul is sure. That's the thing to understand about him. He's a devout, brilliant Pharisee, and he's certain these followers of Jesus are dangerous.
After Stephen, he goes house to house in Jerusalem, dragging people off to prison. Then he asks the high priest for letters so he can do the same in Damascus, far to the north.
He's on the road, nearly there, when a light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground. And a voice, in the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?"

teach.b: Saul asks who's speaking. The answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Not my followers.
Me. Catholics hear this as the heart of what the Church is, the body of Christ: hurt his people and you hurt him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and can't see a thing.

His companions lead him by the hand into Damascus, where he sits three days without eating or drinking. Meanwhile, the Lord speaks to a disciple in Damascus named Ananias: go to Saul. Ananias, very reasonably, objects.
This man? The one who came here to arrest us? Go, he's told; he's my chosen instrument.

So Ananias goes, and his first words to the man who came to put him in chains are: "Brother Saul." He lays his hands on him, and "immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight."
That's where the phrase comes from: the scales fell from my eyes. Two things the story doesn't say.
There's no horse: Saul falls to the ground, but the horse comes from later paintings. And God doesn't rename him on the road.

teach.h: THERE FELL FROM HIS EYES AS IT WERE SCALES.
teach.b: A few chapters later Acts simply says Saul was also called Paul, and from then on Luke uses Paul; some readers take them as his Jewish and Roman names.
The man who came to Damascus to put people in chains spends the rest of Acts carrying the name he tried to silence. Catholics keep the feast of his conversion on January twenty-fifth.

how: Catholics keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on 25 January, and many use the phrase a Damascus road for any sudden turning of heart.

games.q: you're Ananias. the Lord tells you to go to the man who came to Damascus to arrest you. what do you do?
games.why: he objects honestly, then goes, and his first words are "brother Saul."

practice: Saul wasn't a bad man trying to do wrong; he was sure he was right. So think of something you're very sure about, especially about a person or a group, and ask gently, without forcing an answer: is there anything I'm not seeing?
Then think of Ananias: is there someone you'd be afraid to call brother or sister? If you pray, you can ask to see.

wordCard.voice: Ananias. The disciple in Damascus sent to lay hands on Saul, the man he'd feared, and call him brother.
